text.title: An Encounter
text.author: James Joyce
text.description: Two schoolboys, the narrator and Mahony, skip school for a day of adventure in Dublin, planning to visit the Pigeon House. Their outing is interrupted by an unsettling encounter with a mysterious older man in a field near Ringsend.

narrator.name: The Narrator
narrator.description: A schoolboy who skips school for a day of adventure with Mahony. He is introspective, imaginative, and conflicted between his desire for adventure and his fear of authority.
narrator.context: The narrator is one of the younger, more timid boys in Joe Dillon's circle. He prefers detective stories to Wild West tales and is afraid of seeming studious.

data.physicalDescription: Young boy with frail canvas shoes that he has pipeclayed

mahony.name: Mahony
mahony.description: A schoolboy and friend of the narrator. He is bold, playful, uses slang freely, and is more physically adventurous than the narrator.
mahony.context: Mahony is the narrator's companion on the day of truancy. He is dark-complexioned and wears a cricket club badge. He is more willing to engage in rough play and mischief.

data.physicalDescription: Dark-complexioned boy wearing a silver cricket club badge in his cap

joe-dillon.name: Joe Dillon
joe-dillon.description: A schoolboy who introduces the Wild West to the narrator and his friends through his collection of magazines. He is fierce, energetic, and later becomes a priest.
joe-dillon.context: Joe Dillon is the leader of the boys' games and the source of their Wild West adventures. His parents attend eight-o'clock mass every morning on Gardiner Street.

data.physicalDescription: Looks like an Indian when he capers around the garden with an old tea-cosy on his head

leo-dillon.name: Leo Dillon
leo-dillon.description: Joe Dillon's younger brother. He is fat, idle, and timid. He is caught reading The Halfpenny Marvel in class and later backs out of the truancy plan.
leo-dillon.context: Leo Dillon is Joe's younger brother and one of the original three boys planning the day of truancy. He is more cautious and ultimately does not participate.

data.physicalDescription: Fat young boy with a confused puffy face

father-butler.name: Father Butler
father-butler.description: A schoolmaster who discovers Leo Dillon reading The Halfpenny Marvel and rebukes him severely. He represents school authority and moral disapproval.
father-butler.context: Father Butler is a teacher at the boys' school who enforces discipline and moral standards. He is dismissive of adventure literature.

mysterious-man.name: The Mysterious Man
mysterious-man.description: An older man encountered by the narrator and Mahony in a field near Ringsend. He is shabbily dressed, speaks obsessively about girls and whipping, and makes the boys deeply uncomfortable.
mysterious-man.context: The man appears in the field where the boys rest. His behavior becomes increasingly disturbing as he speaks about girls and whipping in a repetitive, obsessive manner.

data.physicalDescription: Fairly old with ashen-grey moustache, shabbily dressed in greenish-black suit, wearing a jerry hat with high crown, bottle-green eyes, yellow teeth with great gaps

mrs-dillon.name: Mrs. Dillon
mrs-dillon.description: Joe Dillon's mother. She is mentioned only briefly as having a peaceful odour.
mrs-dillon.context: Mrs. Dillon attends eight-o'clock mass every morning on Gardiner Street with her husband.

mr-dillon.name: Mr. Dillon
mr-dillon.description: Joe Dillon's father. He is mentioned only briefly as attending mass with his wife.
mr-dillon.context: Mr. Dillon attends eight-o'clock mass every morning on Gardiner Street with his wife.

mahonys-sister.name: Mahony's Sister
mahonys-sister.description: Mahony's older sister who is supposed to write an excuse for Mahony's absence from school.
mahonys-sister.context: She is part of the plan to cover up the boys' truancy by writing a false excuse.

leo-dillon-brother.name: Leo Dillon's Brother
leo-dillon-brother.description: Leo Dillon's older brother (Joe Dillon) who is supposed to say Leo is sick to cover his absence.
leo-dillon-brother.context: He is part of the plan to cover up Leo's truancy.

mr-ryan.name: Mr. Ryan
mr-ryan.description: A teacher or authority figure at the school who is expected to punish Leo Dillon.
mr-ryan.context: He is mentioned as someone who would punish Leo Dillon at three o'clock.

ragged-girls.name: Ragged Girls
ragged-girls.description: A group of poor girls encountered by Mahony and the narrator on Wharf Road.
ragged-girls.context: They are chased by Mahony and later scream insults at the boys.

ragged-boys.name: Ragged Boys
ragged-boys.description: A group of poor boys who throw stones at Mahony and the narrator.
ragged-boys.context: They throw stones at the narrator and Mahony out of chivalry toward the ragged girls.

labourers.name: Labourers
labourers.description: Working men encountered at the quays and on the ferryboat.
labourers.context: They are seen eating lunches at the quays and traveling on the ferryboat.

little-jew.name: Little Jew
little-jew.description: A Jewish man encountered on the ferryboat with a bag.
little-jew.context: He travels on the ferryboat with the narrator and Mahony.

green-eyed-sailor.name: Green-Eyed Sailor
green-eyed-sailor.description: A tall sailor on the Norwegian vessel who calls out cheerfully as planks fall.
green-eyed-sailor.context: He is observed by the narrator who is looking for someone with green eyes.

bystander.name: Bystander
bystander.description: An unnamed bystander who identifies the Norwegian vessel.
bystander.context: He provides information about the ship's nationality.

cat.name: Cat
cat.description: A cat that Mahony chases in Ringsend and later in the field.
cat.context: The cat serves as a distraction for Mahony during the encounter with the mysterious man.

north-richmond-st.name: North Richmond Street
north-richmond-st.description: A street in Dublin where the narrator lives. He hides his books in the long grass near the ashpit at the end of his garden.
north-richmond-st.context: The narrator lives on this street and it is his starting point for the day of truancy.

dillon-back-garden.name: Joe Dillon's Back Garden

dillon-back-garden.context: This is where the boys gather every evening after school to play games inspired by Wild West literature.

dillon-house.name: Dillon House

dillon-house.context: The Dillon family home where the boys gather for games. The parents attend eight-o'clock mass every morning.

canal-bank.name: Canal Bank
canal-bank.description: The bank of the canal where the narrator walks on his way to the bridge.
canal-bank.context: The narrator hurries along the canal bank on his way to the bridge.

north-strand-road.context: The boys walk along this road toward the Vitriol Works.

vitriol-works.name: Vitriol Works
vitriol-works.description: An industrial facility in Dublin that the boys pass on their way to the Wharf Road.
vitriol-works.context: The boys pass this industrial site on their journey toward the quays.

wharf-road.name: Wharf Road

wharf-road.context: The boys walk along this road as part of their planned route to the Pigeon House.

smoothing-iron.context: The boys attempt to arrange a siege at this location but find they need at least three people.

liffey-ferryboat.name: Liffey Ferryboat

liffey-river.name: Liffey River

dodder-field.name: Field near the Dodder
dodder-field.description: A field near the Dodder River where the boys rest and encounter the mysterious man.
dodder-field.context: The boys reach this field after exploring Ringsend. It is here that they encounter the mysterious man.

gardiner-street.name: Gardiner Street

pluck-magazine.context: One of the magazines in Joe Dillon's library.

raspberry-lemonade.description: Bottles of raspberry lemonade that the boys buy in a huckster's shop.
raspberry-lemonade.context: The boys buy a bottle of raspberry lemonade each to refresh themselves.

green-stems.culturalSignificance: Represents folk traditions and childhood games

stick.name: Stick
stick.description: A stick that the mysterious man carries and taps on the ground.
stick.context: The man walks with a stick in one hand, tapping it on the turf lightly.
stick.culturalSignificance: Represents the man's deliberate, measured approach

jerry-hat.name: Jerry Hat
jerry-hat.description: A hat with a high crown that the mysterious man wears.
jerry-hat.context: The man wears a jerry hat with a high crown.

greenish-black-suit.name: Greenish-Black Suit
greenish-black-suit.description: A shabbily dressed suit in greenish-black that the mysterious man wears.
greenish-black-suit.context: The man is shabbily dressed in a suit of greenish-black.
greenish-black-suit.culturalSignificance: Represents the man's shabby, unkempt appearance

cricket-club-badge.name: Silver Cricket Club Badge

textMentions: silver badge of a cricket club
cricket-club-badge.context: Mahony wears this badge in his cap, which causes ragged children to think he and the narrator are Protestants.
cricket-club-badge.culturalSignificance: Represents religious and social identity in Dublin

metal-piping.name: Metal Piping
metal-piping.description: Metal piping beside the river where the boys sit to eat their currant buns.
metal-piping.context: The boys sit on metal piping beside the river to eat their lunch.

books.context: The narrator hides his books in the long grass near the ashpit at the end of his garden.
books.culturalSignificance: Represents the narrator's rejection of school authority

e01-dillon-introduces-wild-west.description: Joe Dillon introduces the Wild West to the boys through his collection of magazines including The Union Jack, Pluck, and The Halfpenny Marvel.

e02-dillon-war-dance.description: Joe Dillon performs a war dance of victory after the boys' battles, wearing a tea-cosy on his head and beating a tin with his fist.

e03-dillon-vocation.description: It is reported that Joe Dillon has a vocation for the priesthood, which surprises everyone.

e04-spirit-unruliness.description: A spirit of unruliness diffuses itself among the boys, causing them to band together despite differences.

e05-narrator-preference.description: The narrator reveals his preference for American detective stories featuring beautiful girls over Wild West tales.

e06-leo-dillon-caught.description: Leo Dillon is discovered with a copy of The Halfpenny Marvel during Father Butler's Roman History class.

e07-father-butler-rebuke.description: Father Butler rebukes Leo Dillon for reading The Halfpenny Marvel, calling it rubbish and expressing surprise at educated boys reading such material.

e08-narrator-hunger.description: The narrator reflects that despite the school's restraining influence, he hungers for wild sensations and real adventures that must be sought abroad.

e09-plan-miching.description: The narrator, Mahony, and Leo Dillon plan a day of miching (truancy) to visit the Pigeon House, each saving sixpence.

e10-collect-sixpence.description: The narrator collects sixpence from Mahony and Leo Dillon, showing them his own sixpence.

e11-eve-arrangements.description: The boys make final arrangements on the eve of their adventure, shake hands, and express excitement.

e12-bad-sleep.description: The narrator sleeps badly the night before the adventure.

e13-hide-books.description: The narrator hides his books in the long grass near the ashpit at the end of his garden and hurries along the canal bank.

e14-bridge-arrival.description: The narrator arrives at the Canal Bridge on a mild sunny morning in the first week of June and sits on the coping, admiring his pipeclayed canvas shoes.

e15-mahony-arrives.description: Mahony arrives at the bridge, smiling, and climbs up beside the narrator.

e16-mahony-catapult.description: Mahony brings out his catapult and explains improvements he has made to it, saying he brought it to have 'gas' with the birds.

e17-leo-dillon-funk.description: Mahony realizes that Leo Dillon has backed out of the plan, saying 'I knew Fatty'd funk it.'

e18-forfeit-sixpence.description: Mahony and the narrator claim Leo Dillon's sixpence as forfeit, giving them more money for their adventure.

e19-walk-north-strand.description: Mahony and the narrator walk along North Strand Road until they come to the Vitriol Works, then turn right along Wharf Road.

e20-mahony-indian-play.description: Mahony begins to play the Indian as soon as they are out of public sight.

e21-ragged-girls-chase.description: Mahony chases a crowd of ragged girls, brandishing his unloaded catapult.

e22-stone-throwing.description: Two ragged boys throw stones at Mahony and the narrator out of chivalry toward the girls.

e23-swaddlers-insult.description: The ragged troop screams 'Swaddlers!' after the boys, thinking they are Protestants because of Mahony's cricket club badge.

e24-smoothing-iron-siege.description: The boys arrange a siege at the Smoothing Iron but find it is a failure because they need at least three people.

e25-near-river.description: The boys walk through noisy streets flanked by high stone walls, watching cranes and engines, and being shouted at by cart drivers.

e26-currant-buns.description: At noon, the boys buy two big currant buns and sit down to eat them on metal piping beside the river.

e27-commerce-spectacle.description: The boys observe Dublin's commerce, including barges, fishing fleets, and a big white sailing-vessel being discharged.

e28-mahony-run-away.description: Mahony says it would be right 'skit' to run away to sea on one of the big ships.

e29-geography-substance.description: The narrator sees the geography he learned at school gradually taking substance under his eyes as he looks at the high masts.

e30-cross-liffey.description: The boys cross the Liffey in the ferryboat, paying their toll, traveling with two labourers and a little Jew with a bag.

e31-norwegian-vessel.description: The boys observe a graceful threemaster being discharged, which a bystander identifies as a Norwegian vessel.

e32-green-eyes-sailor.description: The narrator examines the foreign sailors looking for someone with green eyes, but finds only a tall sailor with possibly green eyes who calls out cheerfully.

e33-ringsend-wandering.description: The boys wander slowly into Ringsend, buying biscuits, chocolate, and raspberry lemonade in the squalid streets where fishermen's families live.

e34-cat-chase.description: Mahony chases a cat down a lane, but the cat escapes into a wide field.

e35-field-rest.description: The boys reach a field with a sloping bank overlooking the Dodder and rest there, both feeling tired.

e36-pigeon-house-abandoned.description: The boys decide it is too late and they are too tired to carry out their project of visiting the Pigeon House.

e37-man-appears.description: A mysterious man approaches from the far end of the field, walking slowly with a stick, dressed shabbily in a greenish-black suit and jerry hat.

e38-man-sits-down.description: The man sits down beside the boys on the slope slowly and with great care.

e39-weather-talk.description: The man talks about the weather, saying it will be a very hot summer, and reflects on how the seasons have changed since his schoolboy days.

e40-books-discussion.description: The man asks if the boys have read Thomas Moore, Sir Walter Scott, and Lord Lytton, and the narrator pretends he has read every book mentioned.

e41-narrator-pretends.description: The narrator pretends to have read all the books the man mentions to avoid seeming stupid.

e42-mahony-games.description: The man says Mahony is different from the narrator, going in for games rather than books.

e43-sweethearts-question.description: The man asks which of the boys has the most sweethearts. Mahony mentions he has three 'totties' and the narrator says he has none.

e44-man-liberal-attitude.description: The man expresses a liberal attitude about boys having sweethearts, saying 'Every boy has a little sweetheart.'

e45-man-monologue.description: The man speaks obsessively about girls' hair and hands in a repetitive, monotonous voice, circling around the same ideas.

e46-man-leaves.description: The man stands up slowly and says he has to leave for a minute or so, walking slowly away toward the near end of the field.

e47-mahony-exclaims.description: Mahony exclaims 'I say! Look what he's doing!' and later calls the man 'a queer old josser!'

e48-narrator-names.description: The narrator suggests they use false names, saying 'let you be Murphy and I'll be Smith.'

e49-man-returns.description: The man comes back and sits down beside the narrator again.

e50-mahony-chases-cat.description: Mahony catches sight of the cat that had escaped him earlier and pursues her across the field, then wanders aimlessly at the far end.

e51-man-speaks-whipping.description: The man speaks to the narrator about chastising boys, saying rough boys ought to be whipped and well whipped.

e52-man-monologue-whipping.description: The man continues his monologue, describing in detail how he would whip boys who talk to girls or have sweethearts, speaking with an almost affectionate voice.

e53-narrator-stands.description: The narrator stands up abruptly after the man's monologue pauses.

e54-narrator-shoe-pretense.description: The narrator delays a few moments pretending to fix his shoe properly to hide his agitation.

e55-narrator-goodbye.description: The narrator says he is obliged to go and bids the man good-day.

e56-narrator-fear.description: The narrator goes up the slope calmly but with his heart beating quickly with fear that the man will seize him by the ankles.

e57-narrator-calls-murphy.description: The narrator calls loudly across the field 'Murphy!' with an accent of forced bravery.

e58-mahony-responds.description: Mahony sees the narrator and hallooes in answer.

e59-mahony-runs.description: Mahony runs across the field toward the narrator as if to bring him aid.

e60-narrator-penitence.description: The narrator realizes he is penitent, for in his heart he had always despised Mahony a little.

Formalist Reading.name: Formalist Reading
Formalist Reading.description: A formalist analysis of 'An Encounter' focusing on narrative structure, literary devices, symbolism, and the formal properties of the text itself. This reading emphasizes how Joyce constructs meaning through language, form, and the interplay of narrative perspective, examining the story's technical achievement rather than biographical or historical context.

theme-disillusionment.name: Disillusionment and Failed Escape
theme-disillusionment.description: The progressive deflation of romantic expectation through structural irony. The boys' quest for adventure culminates not in triumph but in fear and retreat, mirroring the formal movement from aspiration to paralysis.

theme-narrative-unreliability.name: Narrative Unreliability and Self-Deception
theme-narrative-unreliability.description: The narrator's tendency to misrepresent reality through pretense and imagination, formally enacted through his internal monologue and the gap between his perceptions and objective events.

theme-paralysis.name: Paralysis and Inaction
theme-paralysis.description: The formal structure enacts a movement toward stasis and inability to act. Characters are repeatedly blocked, delayed, or diverted from their goals, creating a pattern of frustrated agency.

theme-language-power.name: Language as Power and Seduction
theme-language-power.description: The mysterious man's hypnotic, repetitive language functions formally as a stylistic device that mirrors his predatory intent. Language becomes a tool of manipulation and control.

sym-pigeon-house.name: The Pigeon House
sym-pigeon-house.description: A formal symbol of the unreachable goal. Its absence from the narrative—the boys never arrive—creates a structural void that defines the story's movement toward failure and retreat.

currentMeanings.description: Unattainable aspiration and the gap between desire and achievement
The formal principle of narrative incompleteness

sym-magazines.name: Adventure Magazines (Union Jack, Pluck, Halfpenny Marvel)
sym-magazines.description: Formal representations of literary fantasy and escapism. Their presence in the narrative establishes the gap between textual imagination and lived reality, a central formal concern.

currentMeanings.description: The seductive power of narrative and imagination
The inadequacy of literary fantasy to satisfy real desire

sym-mysterious-man.name: The Mysterious Man
sym-mysterious-man.description: A formal embodiment of the uncanny and the repressed. His appearance disrupts the narrative's tone and introduces a new register of language and threat, functioning as the story's formal climax.

currentMeanings.description: The intrusion of adult sexuality and danger into childhood innocence
The power of obsessive language and repetition to create unease
The formal principle of narrative disruption and tonal shift

sym-canvas-shoes.name: Pipeclayed Canvas Shoes
sym-canvas-shoes.description: A formal symbol of the narrator's self-consciousness and performative identity. His attention to these shoes marks his awareness of appearance and social presentation, reinforcing themes of pretense.

currentMeanings.description: The narrator's concern with external presentation and social performance
Fragility and vulnerability masked by careful preparation

symrel-magazines-pigeon-house.name: Fantasy and Unattainable Reality
symrel-magazines-pigeon-house.description: The magazines represent the boys' imaginative aspirations, while the Pigeon House represents the real world goal they cannot reach. The formal gap between these creates the story's central irony.
symrel-magazines-pigeon-house.nature: Literary fantasy cannot bridge the distance between desire and achievement; imagination fails in the face of physical and social reality.
symrel-magazines-pigeon-house.interpretation: Literary fantasy cannot bridge the distance between desire and achievement; imagination fails in the face of physical and social reality.

symrel-man-language.name: Predatory Language and Obsession
symrel-man-language.description: The mysterious man's repetitive, hypnotic monologues formally enact his predatory nature through stylistic means. His language becomes a weapon of seduction and control.
symrel-man-language.nature: The formal properties of language—repetition, rhythm, obsessive circling—can be instruments of psychological manipulation and threat.
symrel-man-language.interpretation: The formal properties of language—repetition, rhythm, obsessive circling—can be instruments of psychological manipulation and threat.

symrel-shoes-pretense.name: Appearance and Self-Deception
symrel-shoes-pretense.description: The narrator's attention to his pipeclayed shoes parallels his tendency to pretend and misrepresent himself throughout the narrative, creating a formal pattern of performative identity.
symrel-shoes-pretense.nature: The careful maintenance of external appearance mirrors the narrator's careful construction of false narratives about himself and his experiences.
symrel-shoes-pretense.interpretation: The careful maintenance of external appearance mirrors the narrator's careful construction of false narratives about himself and his experiences.

narrator.name: The Narrator (Unnamed Schoolboy)
narrator.description: A first-person narrator whose perspective is limited and unreliable. He is introspective and imaginative, but his narration reveals significant gaps between his self-perception and objective reality. His voice is formal and literary, employing sophisticated vocabulary and complex sentence structures that contrast with his youth.

reader.name: The Implied Formalist Reader
reader.description: A reader attentive to narrative structure, literary devices, and the formal properties of the text. This reader recognizes irony, symbolism, and the gap between narrative voice and narrative events. They appreciate Joyce's technical mastery and the way form enacts meaning.

author.name: James Joyce
author.description: A modernist author employing sophisticated narrative techniques, including unreliable narration, stream of consciousness, and symbolic imagery. Joyce constructs meaning through formal properties of language and narrative structure rather than explicit authorial commentary.
